data.title: Lease
data.tagline: A lease is time-limited ownership that must be renewed and can be taken over after it expires
data.learningOutcome: You can explain acquire, renew, expiry, and takeover, and require a monotonically increasing fencing token so the write target rejects stale holders.
data.description: If two scheduler instances can run the daily summary, one can acquire and renew a lease while the other waits. If the holder fails, the lease expires and a waiting instance can take over. A lease only decides who may take over: a delayed old holder can still write, so each takeover also needs a larger fencing token that the write target checks atomically to reject stale holders.

learning.assumes: You know the same job can be triggered by multiple service instances.
learning.outcome: You can explain acquire, renew, expiry, and takeover, and require a monotonically increasing fencing token so the write target rejects stale holders.

distinctions.label: Lock
distinctions.explanation: A standard Lock requires explicit release and may deadlock on node crash; a Lease adds TTL and heartbeat renewals for automatic failover.

explanation.title: Control takeover with renewal and expiry
explanation.text: Without coordination, both schedulers can start the daily summary. A lease lets only the current holder run and renew ownership. If it fails or disconnects, a waiting instance must wait for expiry before acquiring a new lease and taking over.

explanation.title: Verify the old-holder risk
explanation.text: Each successful takeover receives a larger fencing token, and the database or target service compares it atomically when accepting a write. Pause A through expiry, let B take over, then resume A and verify that A's stale write is rejected.

explanation.title: Another case: controller leadership
explanation.text: When several controllers can update the same resources, a lease can elect the current leader and be renewed. After failure, a new controller takes over with a newer token so the old leader cannot keep submitting changes.

data.boundary: A lease is not a permanent lock, and one late heartbeat is not proof of expiry. Checking ownership before a write still leaves a check-then-write gap. To stop an expired holder, the write target must atomically validate a monotonically increasing fencing token, or use an equivalent stale-request rejection mechanism.

lessonPractice.title: The current scheduler is unreachable and another instance is ready to run the same job. When may it take over?

options.label: Confirm expiry, acquire a larger fencing token, and have the write target atomically reject stale tokens
options.feedback: Correct. Expiry permits takeover, while the monotonically increasing token lets the write target reject a recovered old holder.

options.label: Wait forever unless the old instance releases the lease itself
options.feedback: A lease lets an unreachable holder lose ownership eventually; waiting forever prevents recovery.

options.label: Ignore lease state and start as soon as one heartbeat is late
options.feedback: A short network delay is not expiry; immediate takeover can run the job twice.

data.agentPrompt: Use a lease for the daily summary job: an instance acquires time-limited ownership and renews it while running; after expiry, the new holder receives a larger fencing token. Make the database or target service atomically reject writes whose token is older than the current one. Pause instance A until expiry, let B take over and write, then resume A; verify that A's stale write is rejected and only B's result is accepted.

references.title: Use fencing tokens to reject expired holders
